points.text: Caches save copies of responses so that subsequent requests for the same resource don't need to contact the original server.
points.quote: A cache stores a copy of a response so that later requests for the same resource can be answered without contacting the origin server.

points.text: The Cache-Control header dictates how caches should operate.
points.quote: The Cache-Control response header tells caches how to behave.

points.text: The max-age directive specifies the duration, in seconds, that a response remains considered fresh.
points.quote: The max-age directive sets how many seconds a response stays fresh.

points.text: The ETag header provides a unique identifier for a particular version of a resource.
points.quote: The ETag header carries an identifier for a specific version of a resource.

points.text: The no-store directive mandates that a response cannot be saved in any cache.
points.quote: The no-store directive means a response must not be kept in any cache.

points.text: The private directive restricts a response to being stored only in the individual user's browser cache.
points.quote: The private directive limits a response to the user's own browser cache.

examples.title: Basic Caching for Speed
examples.scenario: Imagine you frequently visit a news website and want the pages to load instantly.
steps: The first time you visit, the website sends the page content to your browser cache.
On subsequent visits, your browser checks its cache and serves the stored copy immediately.
examples.quote: A cache stores a copy of a response so that later requests for the same resource can be answered without contacting the origin server.

examples.title: Protecting Sensitive Information
examples.scenario: You are viewing your bank account balance online and do not want any intermediary system to save this data.
steps: The server sends the account page with the no-store directive.
Any cache, including shared ones, is instructed not to save this response.
examples.quote: The no-store directive means a response must not be kept in any cache.

examples.title: Forcing Revalidation
examples.scenario: You are viewing a product page where the price changes frequently, so you need the latest information.
steps: The server sends the product page with the no-cache directive.
Your browser is allowed to store the page, but it must check with the server before showing it again.
examples.quote: The no-cache directive does not mean "do not cache".

audio.speaker: Ana
audio.text: Basically, a cache keeps a copy of a response so it doesn't have to bother the origin server for the same thing again.
audio.quote: A cache stores a copy of a response so that later requests for the same resource can be answered without contacting the origin server.

audio.speaker: Ben
audio.text: The Cache-Control header is what tells caches exactly how they should act.
audio.quote: The Cache-Control response header tells caches how to behave.

audio.speaker: Ana
audio.text: The max-age directive specifies how long a response is considered fresh.
audio.quote: The max-age directive sets how many seconds a response stays fresh.

audio.speaker: Ana
audio.text: To check for changes, the ETag header holds an ID for a specific version of the resource.
audio.quote: The ETag header carries an identifier for a specific version of a resource.

audio.speaker: Ben
audio.text: If nothing has changed, the server sends back a 304 status with no body, which saves bandwidth.
audio.quote: If the resource has not changed, the server replies with status 304 Not Modified and no body, which saves bandwidth.

audio.speaker: Ana
audio.text: The no-store directive is strict: it means a response absolutely cannot be kept in any cache.
audio.quote: The no-store directive means a response must not be kept in any cache.

audio.speaker: Ben
audio.text: It's important to know that the no-cache directive doesn't actually mean 'do not cache'.
audio.quote: The no-cache directive does not mean "do not cache".
